newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurocourt to rule on UK's Saunders trial.
newsitem.headline: Eurocourt to rule on UK's Saunders trial.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights will rule on Tuesday whether Britain denied a fair trial to Ernest Saunders, former chairman of the Guinness plc drinks group, who was convicted of fraud in 1990.
A ruling against Britain could force it to pay compensation to Saunders and rein in the power of fraud investigators.
It would also embarrass London, smarting from a string of recent court condemnations including for the killings of three Irish guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988.
Rolv Ryssdal, president of the Strasbourg-based court, will announce the court's ruling on Saunders' allegations at 10.30 a.m. (0930 GMT) on Tuesday.

The omens are not good for London since the European Commission of Human Rights, which vets cases for the court, expressed the opinion by 14-1 in 1994 that Britain had violated Saunders' rights by forcing him to give incriminating evidence.
Rulings by the court, a branch of the 40-nation Council of Europe, usually follow the commission's opinions.

Saunders, now 61, was convicted in 1990 on 12 counts including false accounting and theft for inflating Guinness' share price to help its 1986 takeover of whisky group Distillers Plc prevail against rival bidder Argyll Plc.

He contends the trial was unfair because part of the evidence was obtained by Department of Trade and Industry inspectors -- who can force suspects to reply to questions or risk fines and up to two years' jail for contempt.
Saunders, sacked by Guinness in 1987, was sentenced to five years in jail in 1990 but his term was halved in 1991 after doctors found he was suffering from an Alzheimer-type disease.

The commission said in a non-binding opinion in 1994 that: "The privilege allowing a person to avoid self-incrimination plays an important role in protecting suspects from pressures and constraint in penal cases."
British government lawyers argued that a right to silence cannot be absolute, especially for corporate bosses meant to be fully accountable to shareholders.

A ruling against Britain could also lead to similar action by other members of the so-called "Guinness Four" convicted with Saunders -- businessmen Gerald Ronson and Jack Lyons, and financier Tony Parnes.

Britain's Lord Chancellor Lord Mackay of Clashfern visited Strasbourg last month to urge the court to soften enforcement of human rights rules, saying it should not meddle in states' sensitive internal affairs.
The commission angered Britain in September by agreeing to take up the case of a British 12-year-old boy seeking to overturn British laws allowing his parents to spank him.

Earlier this year, for instance, the court condemned Britain's system for jailing minors. Most controversially, last year the court condemned Britain for the killings of three unarmed Irish Republican Army guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988.
